connector: Here’s a question before we open the book: what if every time someone else broke a rule, you got in trouble for it? In today’s chapters you’ll meet a boy whose whole job is exactly that. Watch who gives the orders, who gets punished, and how each boy feels about it.

cards.title: Why a Whipping Boy?
cards.sub: A real prince, and the rule in this book
cards.look: A painting of a real English prince named Edward. It was painted about 500 years ago, when he was about one year old. The words at the bottom are in Latin, an old language.

art.alt: A painting of a baby prince in a red and gold outfit and a feathered hat
art.title: Edward VI as a Child

text: In this book, nobody is allowed to spank a prince. So the king keeps a boy from the streets in the castle, to be punished in the prince’s place. That boy is called the whipping boy.
Stories say Prince Edward had a friend who took his punishments. Nobody knows for sure if that is true. In The Whipping Boy, it is the rule, and Jemmy is the boy who pays for it.
cards.lookBtn: Tap to learn who this prince was

transcripts.welcome: Hello again, it’s Opti. Today we open a brand-new book, The Whipping Boy. Here’s something to think about: what if you got in trouble every time someone else broke a rule? Hold on to that question. First you’ll warm up your words, then you’ll read the first two chapters, and at the end you’ll decide what you think of the prince.
transcripts.guide1: Before the word work, here’s a little secret. Long words are often built from smaller pieces, the way a castle is built from stones. Today you’ll find two of those pieces and figure out what each one means, before the page tells you. After that come some joining words and some vowel pairs. Take it one step at a time.
transcripts.guide2: Before you open the book: Chapter 1 has a feast, a prank, and a boy in a cold tower. As you read, keep asking yourself who gives the orders, and who has to obey. And listen to how Jemmy talks. He grew up on the city streets, and the author wants you to hear it.
transcripts.guide3: Now it’s your turn to have an opinion. A good claim names a character, says what you think of them, and hints at why. You can pick any character, as long as the book gives you a reason. Think back over the feast and the lessons. Then write your claim in one strong sentence.
transcripts.card-whip: This little prince was real. His name was Edward, and he lived in England about five hundred years ago. Stories say a friend of his took his punishments, but nobody knows if that’s true. In our book, it’s the rule, and Jemmy is the one who pays.
transcripts.card-street: Jemmy talks like the streets he grew up on. Words like ain’t and me rags aren’t mistakes. The author wrote them on purpose so you can hear Jemmy in your head. Tap each one to find out what it means.

notes.wgrd: Good readers notice who has power at the start of a story: who gives the orders, and who has to obey.
vocab: a strong feeling of frustration that has been building up
feeling truly sorry and ashamed for something you did wrong
done in a bold, refusing-to-obey way
notes.wordParts: inter- means “between” (interrupt, interact, international). sub- means “under” (submarine).
notes.grammar: A conjunction is a joining word. and adds an idea, but shows a difference, and so shows a result.
notes.spelling: A vowel team is two vowels that make one sound, like ai in rain. A team stays together in one syllable: rain·bow, sea·son.

mods.script: [warmly] Here's a trick good readers use. They ask, who's in charge here? This book has a king, a spoiled prince, and a boy named Jemmy who has no power at all. So while you read, watch for three things. Who gives the orders? Who has to obey? And who gets punished when the prince does something wrong? You don't need to write anything. Just keep those questions in your head.
mods.todo: Listen to Opti. Keep his three questions in your head while you read.

mods.script: Let's fix a sentence. First, look at the correct one at the top. Someone is talking, so the words they say go inside quotation marks. The first word they say gets a capital letter. The king is shouting, so an exclamation mark goes inside the closing quotation mark. Tap the yellow parts to see each rule. Then pick Sentence A or Sentence B, and type it the right way. Look back at the model whenever you need to.
mods.todo: Tap the yellow parts. Then pick Sentence A or B and type it the right way.

mods.script: Long words are often built from smaller parts, like a castle is built from stones. Today's parts are inter and sub. Think of the internet. It connects computers between each other. Now think of a subway. It's a train that runs under the city. So inter means between, and sub means under. Tap See what each part means to check. Then put the parts together, and type each whole word.
mods.todo: Tap See what each part means. Then type each whole word.

mods.script: When you meet a word you don't know, don't skip it. Be a word detective. Let's try exasperation. First, read the sentence around it. The prince is pretending to be sorry, but inside, something is building up toward Jemmy. Next, look at the parts. Asper means rough. So exasperation is a rough, fed-up feeling, like when someone won't stop poking you. Now tap Opti reads it on each card, guess what the word means, and flip the card to check. Then play the matching game.
mods.todo: Listen to each card. Guess the meaning, then flip the card. Then play the matching game.

mods.script: Some little words do a big job. And, but, and so are joining words. They glue two ideas into one sentence. And adds one more idea: I'm hungry and I'm tired. But shows a difference: I'm hungry, but there's no food. So shows what happens next: I'm hungry, so I'll eat. Find the joining word in Jemmy's sentence. Then tap each sentence and drop it in and, but, or so. Say it out loud with each word to hear which one fits.
mods.todo: Find the joining word. Then sort the sentences. Then write three of your own.

mods.script: Some vowels like to work in pairs. When two vowels sit side by side in one beat and make one sound, we call them a vowel team. In feast, the e and the a team up to say ee. In groan, the o and the a say oh. Say each word out loud and clap the beats. Then tap Now name the pattern. Last, sort the words. Two vowels side by side? That's a team.
mods.todo: Tap Now name the pattern. Then say each word, clap its beats, and sort it.

mods.label: Opti shows you how
mods.script: [warmly] This is copia. It means saying one idea in many ways, and it makes you a stronger writer. Watch me try one first, with a different sentence. Jemmy swept the floor. Box one, change the opener: In the cold tower, Jemmy swept the floor. Box two, swap the verb for a stronger one: Jemmy scrubbed the floor. Box three, add a where or a how: Jemmy swept the floor slowly, humming to himself. Same idea, three new ways. Now you try with the king's sentence. Use your own words, not mine.
mods.todo: Write the king’s sentence three new ways, one box at a time.

mods.script: Let's think about Jemmy for a moment. He didn't ask for this job. He was taken off the streets and brought to the castle, just to be punished for someone else. When the prince plays a prank, Jemmy gets twenty whacks, and he doesn't make a sound. Why would he stay quiet? Keep that question in mind as you read.

Time to read Chapters 1 and 2 in your book. Before you start, read the two Pause and Think questions below. They tell you where to stop. Watch for the moment the king shouts, Fetch the whipping boy, and ask yourself why the prince never worries about getting punished. In Chapter 2, watch the prince's lesson. Who is really learning? When you reach each question, stop, think of your answer, and keep reading.
mods.todo: Read the two questions. Then read Ch. 1–2 in your book.

mods.script: Now show what you understood. A good answer does two things. It's a full sentence, and it has a detail from the book. So don't just write, he played a prank. Tell what the prank was. Here are your questions. One, what prank did the prince play at the feast, and what did the guests do? Two, why does the prince call Jemmy the worst whipping boy ever? Three, what does Jemmy secretly hope for, and does it happen? Want a challenge? Pick Scholar, and add one more detail to each answer.
mods.todo: Pick Explorer or Scholar. Answer the three questions in full sentences.

mods.script: Today you'll write a claim. A claim is your opinion, said clearly, with a reason. Meet Clara. Her first idea was, I think the prince is bad. That's a start, but bad doesn't tell us much. So Clara made it stronger: Prince Brat is the most unfair character, because he uses his power to hurt others. See the three parts? A character. What she thinks. And a reason why. Now it's your turn. Pick a character, say what you think, and tell us why.
mods.todo: Write your claim: a character, what you think, and why.

cards.exasperation: Exasperation. Listen to the sentence. But all the while he was feeling a growing exasperation with his whipping boy. Exasperation means a strong feeling of being fed up.
cards.contrite: Contrite. The prince lowered his head so as to appear humbled and contrite. Contrite means truly sorry for something you did wrong. The prince is only pretending.
cards.forbidden: Forbidden. And it was forbidden to spank, thrash, cuff, smack, or whip a prince. Forbidden means not allowed. It's against the rules.
cards.defiantly: Defiantly. Defiantly biting back every yelp and cry, the whipping boy received the twenty whacks. Defiantly means boldly refusing to give in. Jemmy won't cry, because that's what the prince wants.
